text_vader: Big Walk is a game about going on a big walk with your friends. You'll find beautiful sunrises and sunsets, you'll get lost in the bush. You'll find weird items you want to take with you only to have way too few hands to do it. You'll wonder where your friend got off to only to hear from them 15 minutes later after they lost their way and had to find their own radio. Then you'll meet up and chat about the weird puzzle they saw, and decide to go there next. Big Walk isn't fast. It's never fast. And why should it be? Enjoy your time with your friends, walk instead of sprint. Sit around sometimes, just because you can. And talk with your pals when you find them again. text_vader: I am mixed on this game. The devs intentions are extremely noble, and the way they set it out in their main trailer is delightful. But there's so much TEDIUM in this game that makes it hard to recommend. The voice dropoff is a fine idea, if you get seperated you get seperated, but sometimes you cant hear a player in the SAME ROOM AS YOU because its so aggressive. Getting lost in the dark and having to find your friend sounds fun, but without a light the night is pitch black and you cannot see anything. Walking is so slow and takes ages to get anywhere, ten minutes walking through the brush is nice, but then getting there, releasing you needed the whiteboard you left back at main base, and then spending 30 minutes walking there and back is just a slog. There's not enough going on in the game to make that repeated back and forth worthwhile, other than your friends, and the dropoff of voices makes it so that actually trying to hold a conversation and just chat about your day, life, or use it as a hangout game doesnt work. I want to love this game, and I do in parts, the puzzles are delightful, the problem solving is fun (mostly) and theyre all (mostly) fun ("slowly move the ball that prevents you moving while holding it to the other side of the map" can fuck off), but its the in between these that I feel the game falls flat on. It wants to be a "chill by the fire and chat" kinda game, but has too aggressive voice control to enable that, and as a result that falls flat. We ended up getting a movement cheat mod to allow us to just do the puzzles, which is where the game truly shines. EDIT: Don't care where you stand on if ai is ethical to use or not, or if their use is ethical or not. They lied, and did not disclose that they used it. THAT is an issue.

text_vader: ‘Big Walk’ is a game that shines brightest in the details filled in by the players. At its surface it is a jaunt with friends through lovingly recreated Australian bushland. The crux of this game is in the small and unspoken ways it requires collaboration. The act of putting on or using a backpack requires the assistance of friends. The puzzles demand group efforts, with most only requiring two players, so that you can split up into pairs and go wandering off on separate journeys. The primary goal is to collect bulbous shapes, which are never given a canonical name, inviting the players to find their own terms for them. Me and my group speak excitedly of collecting new ‘gourds’, we chant ‘key-key-key’ together when we unlock another section of the map, we sit and listen to the music and watch the sun set, then rise. As an Australian it is remarkable to see my own landscape so lovingly portrayed. I smile whenever I hear the laugh of the kookaburras (my grandmother believes the soul of my great-grandfather are within them), I cherish the sounds of whipbirds, I love the nostalgic sound of white sand that squeaks underfoot on hot Australian beaches. What a fantastic cultural export. On more technical details, the game’s VOIP system works flawlessly. Having just experienced ‘The Outlast Trials’ shoddy in-game voice chat it is a joy to have no tech issues on this front. The game works well on a Steam Deck on ‘high’ graphics settings, although the limitations of the device are felt in its inability to use wired headphones and the in-built mic at the same time. ‘Big Walk’ is a big toy. And it’s the best toy I’ve played with in a long time. EDIT: If you care about the usage of AI to modify 10 lines of code I fear you are perhaps jumping the gun a bit much. Settle down and think about what you really care about.

text_vader: Big Walk is a one-off experience like nothing else. It's clever, cute, genuine, and soulful; and unabashedly designed by human beings with an obvious appreciation for [and understanding of] the chaos and complexity of interpersonal communication. Which, in 2026 (the year that OpenAI started proposing "guardrails") is deeply refreshing... Also, can we talk about how delightful it is to play a game that was designed to be played once, and only once? Don't get me wrong -- there's some fun Roguelite-Card-Battler-Extraction-Shooter-Royales out there. But in an era of gaming when so many titles are published with the hope of going viral and existing forever, with planned DLC's, VIP stores, and Battle Passes hoping to "capture the market", it warms my heart to see people out here makin games that are distinctly NOT designed for infinite replayability or getting people pathologically addicted to them. The world of Big Walk is not procedurally-generated every time you start a new run; it also doesn't require an email, password, access to your kernel, and the forfeiture of your identity to a tech conglomerate that's also funding a g*nocide; and it wasn't made-in-a-corporate-lab to be farmed for clips till it's no longer trending. (Not that they haven't had plenty of positive press.) House House could have spent the last seven years making "a game that keeps you coming back". Instead, they have handcrafted a finite world in which you and a group of (ideally) friends can embark on a unique journey through mind and back; a world where the POIs are only interesting until you have found them, then they're just Points; a world where the puzzles are meant to be solved and then (mostly) forgotten; a world where laughter and frustration and elation are constants; a world where whoever who holds the orb of light can become The One Who Holds The Orb Of Light and whoever's got the best sense of direction becomes Le Navigator Supreme (iykyk); and also a world where the game closes when you press exit. And then, at the end, it's over. That's it. Once you have finished the game, there is no more game. And in my opinion, that sort of finality is a necessary thing to feel every now and then. tldr; idk man, it's real good.

text_vader: So, let's rip the band-aid off: AI was used in this game's development. But would it surprise you that I don't think that's the biggest problem here? Compared to other cases of its use, the use of it in Big Walk is comparatively tiny; used in the closing stages of development and for a problem that seemed unfixable by normal means and was, at least supposedly , only done as a last resort (I say supposedly because people apparently found solutions for it quickly when they were informed of what the problem was, to say nothing of Unity's tech support being laughable at the best of times). In some situations, you could even look past it or come to some degree of understanding, even if it's fairly negative in nature. In the context of something like this, the AI usage is, surprisingly, NOT the main contributor for my negative review (although it definitely does not help its case, natch). The problem lies in the fact that House House decided not to inform its playerbase of this detail right from the start. They may not have needed to at its release time since apparently it was before Steam's AI disclosure thingy became mandatory, but even after that point, no changes on the game's page are visible that discloses this information. If they had provided this detail from the start, there would no doubt be disappointment - but people who could look past it would still play it, and people who would stick to their values would look elsewhere, same as it is in many other cases. But that detail was not made apparent up until a certain point recently with the IGF, and had that certain point not played out the way it did... would House House have let that detail slip at all? Especially baffling since, as indie developers who seemingly took a stance of ethical development (at least, if the other negative reviews here are anything to go by), House House should well have known that dipping your hands into the AI pool in any capacity is considered a poisoned chalice at the best of times these days. I have no clue why they felt that this risk needed to be taken, given the damage to reputation that you risk just by doing so, let alone doing so and keeping quiet about it. Even delaying the game to deal with the issue at hand would have served the game better in the long run (even if folks would get a touch annoyed about it, but they'd more than likely get over it in that case). I'm not of the belief that AI usage itself is what is making people turn against this game and its developers. It's the simple fact that it was used and House House did not see it fit to disclose the information until it was forcibly outed. Some will be more than content to say it's a knee-jerk reaction to AI being used, but this case isn't just an AI-centric issue; people, by nature, don't tend to appreciate being lied to or deceived. And yes, the prior argument about it being before the mandatory disclosures still applies, but a lie of omission is still a lie. What really sucks is that the game - at least, the amount I've experienced with friends - is genuinely fun. But House House have effectively instilled upon themselves a PR nightmare because of a scenario that may well could have been diluted or even avoided outright had they been honest from the beginning - or had been willing to ask out for alternative solutions so as to circumvent whatever problem it was that kicked this chain of events off. As a result of all of this, Big Walk and House House will now have asterisks next to their names and reputations in the wake of Big Walk's controversial revelations. After all, if they were prepared to keep people in the dark about AI usage in this game, then the question has to be asked: what else are they willing to keep us in the dark about? Buyer beware.

text_vader: I'm genuinely surprised how few positive points I have to say about this game. Let's start with the positives: It's cute. Now the bad: Puzzles are extremely repetitive. 80% of the puzzles were very minutely different variations of the same "put tile of shape here when friend describes it." Many puzzles also force your team to split up, cutting off communication (wait, hold on, isn't communication supposed to be the point of the game??) and it's far enough apart that if night falls and you keep moving, you could end up farther away that you started, making the time spent alone almost double. Your character can only hold one item and cannot access their own backpack/hipbag, meaning if you split up with your party (which is mandatory for 80% of the puzzles!!) once you’ve finished the puzzle you have to then meet up with your party without any communication. They tried to remedy this with the tower flare system and I would say “oh that’s fixed then!” if it weren’t for my next point: The world too big. In a game apparently literally made to play and talk with friends, more than 40% of your time is going to be spent alone trekking across the very dark, very monotonous landscape if you play with less than four people, and as someone who played with only one other person, this just made it extremely boring. One small drop from a ledge you didn’t see (see next point) and you’re separated from your group, unable to be heard since proximity chat range is so small, and the very important thing you were holding that is needed to finish the game: IE a literal reward from a puzzle, is now gone and lost in the brush and searching for items is just so frustrating and annoying. With so many items that are necessary to have/ones you want to carry around to have fun, like what you want from a game , my two person team couldn’t have the item scope on us at all times. The game has ZERO accessibility options. Motion blur makes you sick? Too bad. Impaired vision or cheap monitor that could be helped with gamma adjusting (and even for non impaired vision this game is unplayable during night. It’s literally blind wandering) that even the shittiest game has? Yep, no fixing that, you're supposed to use a flashlight or light ball! Yet again on the limited item slots, carrying around a flashlight is like carrying around a dead item for half the time when you already don’t have very much room, so you’re more inclined to just sit and wait for day every time it gets dark. Which is pretty boring when you have to do it every five minutes. The world is also exceedingly empty and not engaging at all. It loses it's "new and exciting" luster by the end of the first tower, and the only time I really got excited was during the black tower and when me and my sister approached the gate. But those moments were so few and far in between that those TWO interesting bits were not enough to carry me through the rest of the game.
